issues.description: The problem statement and UML require Farm to hold animals in a List<Animal> implemented using an ArrayList and initialized in the no-argument constructor, but the provided solution implements the collection as a Queue<Animal> backed by a LinkedList. This is an attribute-type/design mismatch that may confuse students (and any tests) about the expected collection type and how to initialize/use it.
issues.suggestedFix: Make the collection type consistent with the specification: use List<Animal> animals and initialize it as an ArrayList in the no-argument constructor (e.g. this.animals = new ArrayList<>();). Update the getter/setter signatures to use List<Animal>, change addAnimal to animals.add(a), and iterate over the List when singing/feeding. Alternatively, if using Queue/LinkedList is intended, update the problem statement and UML to specify Queue/LinkedList instead.

issues.description: The problem statement explicitly requires the Farm's collection of animals to be a List implemented as an ArrayList, but the provided solution implements the same conceptual attribute as a Queue (backed by LinkedList). The conceptual entity 'collection of animals' is referenced with different type identifiers (List/ArrayList vs Queue/LinkedList) across artifacts. This can confuse students because the instructions ask them to initialize an ArrayList and use List semantics, while the reference solution uses Queue semantics and methods (e.g., offer).
issues.suggestedFix: Align the solution with the problem statement by using List<Animal> as the attribute type and initializing it as a new ArrayList<>() in the no-arg constructor (and update getter/setter signatures to use List). Alternatively, relax the problem wording to permit Queue/LinkedList if that design is intentional; pick one approach and make the same identifier/type choice across problem, template, and solution.
